title: Things to Do in Kohima: War Cemetery, Hornbill Festival, Khonoma & Dzukou
seoTitle: Things to Do in Kohima: Hornbill, Dzukou & More | Kudozz Club
description: Things to do in Kohima: the Kohima War Cemetery, Kisama Heritage Village and the Hornbill Festival, the State Museum, the Cathedral of Reconciliation, the local market, Khonoma green village, the Dzukou Valley trek, Japfu Peak and Naga food.
dek: Nagaland's hill capital, where the Second World War was fought across a tennis court and Naga tribes gather every December for the Hornbill Festival.
searchIntent: Travellers planning two to four days in Kohima, often for the Hornbill Festival or the Dzukou Valley trek.

hero.alt: Memorial at the Kohima War Cemetery
hero.caption: Kohima War Cemetery

intro: Kohima, at about 1,450 metres, is the capital of Nagaland and the home of the Angami Naga. In April to June 1944, the Battle of Kohima halted the Japanese advance into India, with some of the fiercest fighting taking place around the Deputy Commissioner's bungalow and its tennis court. Today the city is a mix of hillside neighbourhoods, churches and markets.

The things to do in Kohima include the War Cemetery, the State Museum, Kisama Heritage Village (the venue of the Hornbill Festival), the green village of Khonoma and treks to the Dzukou Valley and Japfu Peak. Naga food, with its smoked meats, fermented soybean and fiery chillies, is a highlight.
Two days covers the city; four days allows Dzukou and Khonoma. Indian nationals need an Inner Line Permit, available online.
quickAnswer: Attend the Hornbill Festival at Kisama (1–10 December)

Eat smoked pork with bamboo shoot

items.name: Visit the Kohima War Cemetery
body: The War Cemetery, on the slopes of Garrison Hill, holds the graves of over a thousand Commonwealth soldiers. The tennis court lines where the fighting was fiercest are marked in white. The Kohima Epitaph, 'When you go home, tell them of us and say, for your tomorrow, we gave our today', is inscribed on the memorial to the 2nd Division.

items.name: See the Nagaland State Museum
body: The State Museum has displays on the Naga tribes, with costumes, weapons, jewellery, a ceremonial drum and model villages. It is a good way to understand the diversity of Nagaland's communities.

items.name: Visit the Cathedral of Reconciliation
body: The Mary Help of Christians Cathedral on Aradura Hill, built with help from Japanese donors as a symbol of reconciliation after the war, has a large carved wooden crucifix and a distinctive façade inspired by Naga houses.

items.name: Walk through the local market
body: Kohima's local market sells fresh vegetables, chillies, bamboo shoots and more unusual items such as silkworms, snails and river fish, reflecting Naga food traditions.

items.name: Attend the Hornbill Festival

image.alt: Hornbill Festival at Kisama Heritage Village
image.caption: Hornbill Festival

body: The Hornbill Festival, held every year from 1 to 10 December at Kisama Heritage Village about 12 km from Kohima, brings together all the major Naga tribes. Each has a morung (traditional house) at the venue, and there are dances, songs, games, crafts, food stalls and a rock concert in the evenings.
Accommodation in Kohima fills up months in advance; many visitors stay in homestays or camps.

items.name: See Kisama at other times
body: Outside the festival, Kisama Heritage Village is quiet, but the morungs and the World War II museum on site can still be visited.

items.name: Visit Khonoma
body: Khonoma, about 20 km from Kohima, is an Angami village known for its terraced fields, stone gateways and history of resistance to the British in the 19th century. In the 1990s, the villagers banned hunting and logging and set up a conservation sanctuary; it is often described as Asia's first green village. Homestays and guided walks are available.

items.name: Trek to Dzukou Valley

image.alt: Rolling green hills of Dzukou Valley
image.caption: Dzukou Valley

body: Dzukou Valley, on the Nagaland–Manipur border at about 2,400 metres, is a valley of rolling green hills covered in dwarf bamboo, with streams and seasonal flowers, including the endemic Dzukou lily in summer. Treks start from Viswema or Zakhama, a steep climb of three to five hours. Overnight stays are in a basic rest house or tents.

facts.Best time: June to September for flowers; October to March for clear days

items.name: Climb Japfu Peak
body: Japfu Peak, at about 3,000 metres, is the second-highest mountain in Nagaland. A day hike from Kigwema village climbs through forest to the top, with sunrise views over the hills on clear days. The area also has what is often cited as the tallest rhododendron tree in the world.

items.name: See Tuophema village
body: Tuophema, about 40 km from Kohima, has a community-run tourist village with traditional huts, a small museum and cultural programmes, and gives a sense of Angami village life.

items.name: Eat smoked pork and axone
body: Naga cuisine is built around smoked meats, bamboo shoot, axone (fermented soybean) and raja mircha, one of the world's hottest chillies. Try smoked pork with bamboo shoot, galho (a rice and vegetable porridge) and local rice beer. Restaurants in Kohima also serve milder options.

byTraveller.text: Stay for at least three days of Hornbill and add a day at Khonoma.
Dzukou Valley overnight and Japfu Peak for sunrise.
The War Cemetery, the Kisama WWII museum and Khonoma's resistance history.

oneDay: Start at the War Cemetery, then visit the State Museum and the local market. After lunch, drive to Khonoma for a guided village walk, and return to Kohima for Naga food in the evening.
tips: Dimapur, about 75 km away, has the nearest airport and railway station.
Apply for the Nagaland ILP online before travel.
Sundays are quiet; many shops and restaurants close as most of the population attends church.
Ask before photographing people, especially in villages.

faqs.q: What are the best things to do in Kohima?
faqs.a: Visit the War Cemetery and State Museum, attend the Hornbill Festival, visit the Cathedral and local market, see Khonoma, and trek to Dzukou Valley or Japfu Peak.
Every year from 1 to 10 December at Kisama Heritage Village near Kohima.

faqs.q: Do I need a permit for Kohima?
faqs.a: Yes. Indian nationals need an Inner Line Permit for Nagaland.

faqs.q: How hard is the Dzukou Valley trek?
faqs.a: It is a moderate trek with a steep initial climb of about three to five hours from Viswema or Zakhama.
